title: Incident Response in IT and OT
description: How enterprises detect, contain, recover from and report cybersecurity incidents, and why the playbook changes when the systems run factories, pipelines and power grids.
audience: Developers, IT staff and managers who want an enterprise-level picture of incident response; no security background needed.

chapters.title: Highlights
chapters.summary: The lesson in nine cards: the lifecycle, the first 24 hours, the plant that behaves oddly at 2 a.m., and the maths of speed versus damage.

chapters.title: The Incident Response Map
chapters.summary: The response lifecycle, the people and tools involved, and how IT and OT differ, on one map you rebuild from memory.

chapters.title: The First 24 Hours
chapters.summary: You lead the response to a ransomware outbreak: triage, containment, evidence, communication, regulators and the ransom question.

chapters.title: The Night-Shift Anomaly
chapters.summary: A plant's process starts behaving oddly at 2 a.m. Sensor fault, human error or intrusion? Investigate the safe way.

chapters.title: Speed versus Damage
chapters.summary: Play with alert volume, detection time, containment speed, shutdown decisions, recovery bottlenecks and notification clocks.

chapters.title: Response Archipelago
chapters.summary: One island per phase and idea, hands-on activities, then a final exam.

objectives: Describe the incident response lifecycle and who does what in each phase
Make defensible first-day decisions in a ransomware outbreak: triage, containment, evidence, communication
Explain why response changes when the systems run a plant, and what safety-first means in practice
Reason about trade-offs between speed and damage: alerts, detection time, shutdowns, recovery and notification clocks
prerequisites: General IT literacy; no security background needed

glossary.definition: The organised way an organisation detects, contains, removes and recovers from a security incident, then learns from it.
Operational technology: the systems that control physical processes in plants, pipelines and grids.
Stopping an incident from spreading while keeping what you need to investigate and recover.
The record of who held a piece of evidence, when, and what they did with it, so it holds up later.
A layered model of a plant network, from field devices at the bottom to business IT at the top, with a DMZ between.
Independent equipment that forces a process to a safe state when limits are crossed, regardless of other systems.
A legal deadline to report an incident to a regulator or affected people, starting when you become aware of it.
A rehearsal of an incident around a table, following the playbook without touching real systems.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
NIST SP 800-82, Guide to Operational Technology Security
